extracted.intended_audience: brand managers, packaging designers, marketing and communications teams
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative criteria for planning, testing, and executing product packaging redesigns to avoid loss of brand recognition and sales. Focuses on what to change, how much to change, and how to validate changes before launch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't change too much at once
rubrics_metrics.description: The redesign failed because it changed too many elements at once and lost consumer recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only change one or two elements at a time — not the logo, lid, image and slogan all at once. Gradual or staged changes retain recognition; the article cites Coca‑Cola as an example of changing bottle design while keeping core recognizable elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the connection of consumers with the brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Design must respect existing brand identity and the associations consumers have built up over time (e.g., Tropicana's 'premium' association).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which brand cues (words like 'Pure Premium', visual cues, premium signals) are central to consumer perception. If the brand already has a working formula, preserve those cues; if the brand is nascent, first establish a clear brand formula before major redesigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging must be identifiable and complement brand positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Packaging is one of the final communication points and needs to be identifiable and aligned with the overall feeling and positioning of the brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure packaging design supports the brand's positioning (e.g., premium vs basic). Packaging should visually complement advertising and broader brand messaging so it doesn't contradict perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure on-shelf findability — make the product easy to spot
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers did not manage to find the product on supermarket shelves because the new package looked too different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design for quick recognition in a retail environment; avoid changes that require consumers to spend extra time locating the product. Test silhouettes, dominant colors, logo placement and distinctive visual markers against competitor shelves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve key brand cues: logo size, placement, and prominent identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to logo orientation, size and text caused loss of brand association (e.g., Tropicana's logo went vertical and smaller; attention on logo dropped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain logo visibility and other signature elements. Small or differently oriented logos can reduce visual attention; keep brand identifiers prominent enough to sustain brand recall and association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing or ambiguous messaging on packaging
rubrics_metrics.description: New text such as '100% Orange Pure and Natural' confused customers about whether the product or its quality had changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, familiar wording that signals continuity where appropriate. Avoid phrasing that makes consumers question product identity or formulation; if messaging changes, explain or phase it in through other channels first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate new values over time via advertising rather than sudden packaging overhaul
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicating new values is better done over a longer period of time, through advertising, because advertising gives more time and tools to share a story and emotions than package design alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use advertising and campaigns to introduce and validate shifts in brand meaning before embedding them in permanent packaging. Advertising allows iterative feedback and quicker adjustments than packaging changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-test major changes in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Test major packaging changes before executing them to understand impact on recognition and sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-testing platforms (e.g., expoze.io) or consumer testing to predict visual attention and brand recognition. The article argues pre-testing could have revealed the drop in logo attention and prevented the Tropicana failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure visual attention and brand recognition quantitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative attention metrics revealed the new design drew only 2.5% visual attention to the logo versus 10.8% for the old design — a decrease of more than 76%, correlated with sales loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect measurable metrics (visual attention percentages, recognition rates, purchase intent) during testing. Use those metrics to estimate commercial impact — the Tropicana case links reduced attention and consumer confusion to a 20% sales decline and over $50M total loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate changes with realistic context and competitive shelf comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem manifested when the redesigned pack was placed among competitors; consumers either couldn't find it or chose alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test designs in simulated or real shopping contexts and alongside competitors. Evaluate not just isolated aesthetics but competitive distinctiveness, discoverability, and immediate comprehension in situ.
